tagline.text: A Spanish stone church completed in 1849 in the town next to Naga

location.label: Location
location.text: Magarao town center, Camarines Sur (Saint Anne Parish)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: February–May dry season (July 26 feast day, Holy Week events)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~500 (estimate per person for a round trip from Naga plus snacks)

children.text: Magarao Church is the Saint Anne Parish church in the town of Magarao, Camarines Sur, a Spanish colonial stone church begun in 1826 and completed in 1849. It borders Naga City, so it makes an easy half-day add-on to a Naga itinerary.

The formal name of Magarao Church is Saint Anne Parish Church. It stands in the town of Magarao in Camarines Sur province in the Bicol region, and the town shares borders with Naga City, Canaman, Bombon and Libmanan. The name is commonly explained as coming from
garao
, a thorny shrub that once grew abundantly in the area. The population was about 28,000 in the 2024 census, and the town feels more like a quiet working community than a tourist destination.

The church's history goes back to around the 1570s, when Franciscan missionaries first visited the area, and mission work is said to have revived in 1690. It began as a visita (outstation) of the neighboring Canaman parish and became an independent parish in
. After the earthquake of 1811 destroyed the early church, the community used a temporary structure of wood, bamboo and nipa palm, and the present stone church was begun in
and completed in
together with the convent.

Trials continued afterward. The March 1887 earthquake caused heavy damage, and Fr. Vicente Rojo and Fr. Higinio del Alamo repaired the church and convent; typhoons damaged it in 1942 and June 1972, and repairs are recorded in 1948. The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) has declared it a national landmark, and a historical marker installed in 1939 is fixed to a pilaster beside the main entrance. It is a church whose value has long been recognized.

For travelers, this is not a flashy attraction but one stop on a Bicol church circuit. If you visit it after the Naga Metropolitan Cathedral and the Peñafrancia shrine, Bicol's Catholic culture comes across in more depth. The church is small enough to see slowly in a single visit, and if you time it with Mass you can also glimpse everyday local devotion. The town itself is worth a look too. Besides the church, the municipal hall, an old roadside house and the fire station are listed as sights, and Magarao is also known for the traditional healing practice called hilot. Coastal barangays such as Ponong, Barobaybay and Carigsa are said to be served by boats from a wharf near Naga, so if you want to see another side of the town after the church, ask locally how to get there.

The thick stone walls and massive supports from the 1826 start and 1849 completion are still there. It is pleasant to walk once around the exterior while thinking about how the church was rebuilt through a temporary structure after the 1811 earthquake.
The facade has arched openings, pilasters standing on plinths, and decorative cartouches. The pediment holds one arched window and three alcoves, and small finials rise above the outer posts.
A pyramidal roof sits atop the square belfry. Looking up at it while remembering the earthquakes and typhoons Bicol has endured makes the building feel different.

The marker fixed to the pilaster on the gospel side of the main door shows that the church was a conservation target at the national level from early on. An emblem is carved above the marker, so take a closer look.

The interior is distinctive for its synthetic fiberglass panels decorated with sacred imagery and ornamental patterns. It feels different from other colonial churches built mainly of stone and wood, which makes it fun to compare.
The feast of the church's patron saint, Saint Anne, is
July 26
. Parish events take place around then, so it is worth timing a visit if you want to see local life. Programs differ each year, so check with the parish.

In Barangay Santa Lucia in Magarao, a nine-day novena to Saint Lucy is held before her December 13 feast day, and it is known to draw devotees from across Bicol. It is a local event worth knowing about alongside a church visit.
Magarao is described as a town that stages a senakulo, a Passion play, during Holy Week. If you are in Bicol during Holy Week, look up the town's schedule along with your church visit.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: A church visit from central Naga

children.text: Have breakfast in Naga City and find transport to Magarao. Ask at your accommodation for the best way to use a jeepney or tricycle.
Arrive in the town, take photos from in front of the church, and look in turn at the arches, pilasters and alcoves of the facade.
Read the NHCP marker on the pilaster beside the main door, then walk around the belfry and side walls. The thickness of the stone and traces of repair stand out.
If no Mass or prayer is under way, quietly step inside and look at the sacred imagery on the fiberglass panels. Refrain from taking photos during services.
Walk around the market and toward the municipal hall to get a feel for the town, and have a light snack.
Return to Naga City for lunch and continue on to other sights such as the cathedral.
The church is not a place with well-developed signage or a visitor center, so the visit is mostly about walking and looking on your own.
Arrive for a weekday morning Mass at Magarao Church to see local worshippers at their devotions. Check the Mass times before you go.
After seeing the exterior and the historical marker, have breakfast in town.
Move to Naga City and visit the Naga Metropolitan Cathedral and the Marian shrine.
If you have time, link other colonial-era churches or chapels in the area by car. Travel times depend on road conditions, so allow plenty of margin.
From Manila to Naga City, a long-distance bus is the most common option. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so confirm with the operator before departure.
Naga Airport (WNP) is fairly close to Magarao, but routes and flight schedules change often. Check the airline's latest announcements.
You can also fly from Manila to Legazpi Airport and continue overland to Naga.
Departure times and fares from Manila change easily, so confirm the latest information before booking.
Magarao is a town that borders Naga City. The road linking Naga and Calabanga passes through the town.
Jeepneys, tricycles and shared vans run there. Confirm exact routes and fares locally.
Renting a car or using a ride-hailing service such as Grab can save time, but a car may be hard to get on the outskirts of the town.
The area around the church and the town center can be covered comfortably on foot.
It is better to walk in the morning or late afternoon, avoiding the hottest hours.
Seasons matter little for viewing the church exterior, but Bicol is affected by typhoons and the rainy season. The dry months of February–May are the easiest for travel and walking.

If you want to match an event, candidates are the July 26 feast of Saint Anne, the Santa Lucia novena before December 13, and the Holy Week senakulo. At such times, however, crowds can make transport and accommodation congested.

Magarao has few lodgings aimed at tourists. Most travelers stay in Naga City and visit the church from there. Naga has a wide range of hotels and guesthouses to suit different budgets, and Magarao is a short ride away.

Meals are also easier to find in Naga City, where the choice is wider. Bicol cuisine is famous for dishes made with coconut milk and chili, so we suggest trying Bicol food in Naga once and then visiting the church. Around the town market you can pick up simple snacks and drinks.

If the church is your only goal, staying in Naga City is more efficient than booking a room elsewhere. Move out early to catch the morning Mass, then spend the day at Naga's other sights and restaurants; with the short distances, you reduce heat and fatigue. Restaurant and lodging rates vary by season, so check the latest prices when you book.
According to parish notices, Mass is at 6:00 a.m. on weekdays and on Sundays at 6:00 a.m., 7:30 a.m., 4:30 p.m. and other times, but these can change, so check the latest notice before you go.
For parish contact details, check the Archdiocese of Caceres information. For tourism inquiries, you can ask the Naga City investment and tourism office.
Sources differ on some years in the church's history. The 1849 completion, the 1887 earthquake and the 1939 marker are widely confirmed, but for details, defer to on-site information.
Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is expected. During Mass, avoid loud talking and flash photography.
The sun is strong on the town's streets. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and carry enough cash.
Plan it as a half-day trip from Naga and combine it with other churches or the cathedral for better efficiency.
During Holy Week and feast days it gets crowded, so allow plenty of margin for travel.
This is not a place with well-developed tourist facilities, so be sure to confirm opening hours, Mass schedules and transport locally.
The church is a place of worship. Refrain from touring the interior and taking photos during Mass and prayer.
Bicol is a region at risk of typhoons and earthquakes. Check weather advisories and the latest announcements.
Some online sources list the church's location as in Canaman. In map apps, search for Saint Anne Parish, Magarao.
Prices and travel times change with the season, so the amounts in this guide are rough estimates for reference.
Watch for pickpockets and touts, and keep valuables on your person.
The central city of Bicol, bordering Magarao, where lodging, restaurants and transport are concentrated. It is the best starting point for a church visit.
Naga's main church; seeing it together with the Marian shrine rounds out a church circuit itinerary.
Bicol's biggest Marian festival, held in Naga in September. If you can time your trip for it, it is a major sight.
